31.0.0.en: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" [1]

31.0.1.en: Job, in the era before the Law of Moses, was able to rise, with divine help, to a surpassing Gospel-like height. For he did not abstain only from adultery and abominations, but shut the door on sin at the very start of its advance, namely the evil glance. He did not allow himself to look at a virgin in order to desire her, counting this an inward adultery creeping into his senses.

31.0.2.en: God has given us the senses to use as is fitting, a holy gift for which we give thanks to God. But if we misuse them through recklessness and carelessness, we thereby open the door for sin to creep in little by little.

31.0.3.en: For this reason the Fathers of the early Church forbade dwelling together with virgins, however lofty the lives of both parties, not by looking on them as a source of defilement, but for the sake of purity of the eyes, the mind and the heart.

31.0.4.en: * Jeremiah says: [For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces] (Jer 9:21). This happens when desire enters through the senses of the body, and enters into the dwelling of the mind. In contrast to this Isaiah speaks of the righteous: [Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their windows?] (Isa 60:8), for the righteous are said to fly like a cloud, because they rise above the filth of the earth...

31.0.5.en: In order to keep the thoughts of his heart in chastity, Job "made a covenant with his eyes," lest he should see without caution what he might love...

31.0.6.en: Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree if she had not first looked at it without caution, as it is written: "And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to look upon, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat" (Gen 3:6). Therefore we who live a mortal life must set great restraint to limit our gaze toward forbidden things, since the mother of all living (Eve) came to death through the eyes. The prophet also says: [Mine eye affecteth mine heart] (cf. Lam 3:51)... Our Lord said: "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery in his heart" (Mt 5:27-28).

31.0.8.en: * Christ has removed this cause (adultery), since we pay attention even to what is in the heart alone. Now what can they say who share dwelling with virgins? For according to this rule they are guilty of the sin of adultery tens of thousands of times every day, as they look upon them with desire. For this reason blessed Job also laid down this rule from the beginning, removing this kind of glance from himself on every side.

31.0.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:27-28).

31.0.10.en: The lesser righteousness is not committing adultery in deed, while the greater righteousness of the Kingdom of God is not committing adultery at all; then the last commandment came confirming the first, for the Lord did not come to destroy but to fulfill the Law.

31.0.11.en: We must note that He did not say "whosoever desires a woman" but "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her," that is, looks at her with this intention; this look is not the stirring of bodily pleasure but its carrying out, for even though it is restrained, it will be carried out if circumstances permit.

31.0.12.en: For sin is completed in three stages: its provocation, delight in it, and then its satisfaction (its execution).

31.0.13.en: The provocation occurs by means of memory or the senses, such as sight, hearing, smell, taste or touch. If pleasure results from these, it must be restrained. If we were fasting, then at the sight of food the desire to taste is aroused, and this desire produces pleasure. We must not satisfy it but restrain it, if our mind, which keeps us from satisfying it, has the mastery. But if we satisfy it, the sin will be complete in the heart, and God knows of it even if men do not.

31.0.14.en: So these are the steps of sin:

31.0.15.en: The provocation creeps in by means of the bodily senses, as the serpent crept in with the provocation of Eve, for wherever wrong thoughts and imaginations seep into our souls, they spring from outside, from the bodily senses. And if the spirit perceives any hidden sensation apart from these five senses, that sensation is temporary and fleeting. So these imaginations creep into the thought with the cunning of the serpent.

31.0.16.en: The three stages of sin resemble the fall of man recorded in the Book of Genesis: the provocation comes from outside, from the senses, as the serpent caused it; the delight in sin occurs in the bodily desire, as Eve took delight; and the satisfaction of sin occurs in the mind, as in Adam. And because of sin man was expelled from paradise, that is, from the light of the greater righteousness, into death.

31.0.17.en: He who offers pleasure does not force man to accept it, so man must not come down from his lofty rank, in which the mind has the mastery, to a lower rank, for God created man in a rank higher than the animals. Man is not forced to accept pleasure; if he accepts it, he is punished by the just law of God, because he sinned by his own will.

31.0.18.en: However, before sin turns into a habit, there is no pleasure in it, or it is of a slight kind that is made light of, and yielding to it is a great sin as long as this pleasure is forbidden. For he who yields to it does evil in his heart. And after yielding to it and carrying it out, it seems to him that he has satisfied his desire and the matter is finished, but when what provokes it comes again, the pleasure is aroused more strongly than the first time. Yet it is less than the pleasure that results from habit. The pleasure the second time is hard to overcome; nevertheless if he is true to himself, ready for the spiritual war, he will be healed of it, and even of the habit, by the help of his Christ, the Commander of the spiritual battle. Thus the man is subject to Christ and the woman to the man (1 Cor 3:11; Eph 23:5), according to the natural order.

31.1.s.en: 2. His preoccupation with God as his eternal portion

31.1.0.en: "For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high?" [2]

31.1.1.en: The translation of the Jesuit Order has: "What then is the portion from God above, and the inheritance from the Almighty on high?"

31.1.2.en: What is the portion of God, or the heavenly portion on high for the soul, but that the soul sing, saying: "The Lord is my portion, saith my soul" (Lam 3:24)? He who enjoys fellowship with the Lord, and counts the Lord Himself his eternal portion that he enjoys, will not allow his depths to find their delight in earthly things and bodily desires.

31.1.3.en: Many Fathers of the Church see that the virtues are different, interrelated aspects of one truth, which is the enjoyment of fellowship with God. Here Pope Gregory (the Great) links the two verses [1-2] and says that whoever sets in his heart to live pure and chaste, and does not allow the evil glance, enjoys God's support for him in the practice of humility, and his depths are lifted up to seek God Himself as his portion.

31.1.4.en: Every virtue supports the others, and even reveals the beauty of the virtues together, like a heavenly pearl of many facets.

31.1.5.en: * It is as though he were saying clearly: If I defile my mind with thought, I shall not be able to be an heir of Him who is the Author of purity. For nothing can be of any benefit if it is not proved in the eyes of the hidden Judge by the witness of purity. For all the virtues lift themselves up in the eyes of the Creator by mutual help, that is, a virtue without the others becomes either nothing at all, or the least of the virtues. The virtues must be supported by their alliance together. If humility abandons chastity, or chastity leaves humility, before the Author of humility and chastity, what is the use to us of a proud chastity or a defiled humility?

31.1.7.en: Origen the Scholar sees that all the virtues in their essence are the acquiring of the Lord Christ Himself, for man becomes one with Christ; He is the virtue that fills him, He is justice, wisdom and truth. So he who practices virtue shares in the divine nature, or in the characteristics of Christ, as far as the believer can bear.

31.1.8.en: * To seek Christ is like seeking the Word, wisdom, justice, truth and the omnipotence of God. For Christ is all of these.

31.2.0.en: "Is not destruction to the wicked? and a strange punishment (a hideous thing or calamity) to the workers of iniquity!" [3]

31.2.1.en: The Jesuit translation has: "Is not calamity for the unjust, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?"

31.2.2.en: If chastity, represented in the believer's earnestness not to allow an evil glance to creep in upon him, moves him to long for the heavenly reward, where the Lord is his portion, then on the negative side, what does evil or defilement, especially adultery, offer but eternal destruction?

31.2.3.en: By practical experience we taste what the prophet Isaiah said: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked." For sin draws from what is its own, namely corruption, bitterness and ruin, and gives it to those who possess it. It offers to the one who practices it what he has chosen for himself.

31.2.4.en: The wicked man, by his determination upon evil, isolates himself from the holy Church, and so deprives himself of the blessings of the Lord for her, and of her eternal portion in glory.

31.2.5.en: * Let sinners go now, and satisfy the desires of their pleasures. For in the judgment at the end they will feel that in their evil life they were in love with death...

31.2.6.en: Now the righteous man is scourged and corrected with the rod of discipline, because he is being prepared to receive the inheritance of the Father. But let the unjust man go after his pleasures, for he is satisfied with temporal goods to the extent that he is deprived of eternal goods. The unjust man runs toward the death prepared for him, enjoying pleasures without restraint, just as calves prepared for slaughter are left free in the pastures...

31.2.7.en: Let the righteous man weigh well the evils that await the wicked, and not envy him his passing happiness...

31.2.8.en: [Is not banishment for the workers of iniquity?] What we call banishment is exile or "anathema" among the Jews. It will be banishment for the wicked when they find themselves deprived (anathema) of the inheritance of the stern Judge.

31.2.10.en: * The things of grace are accompanied by joy, peace, love and truth... But the forms of sin are accompanied by disturbance, and neither love nor joy toward God.

31.2.11.en: St. Macarius the Great What is meant by sin in Origen's mind?

31.2.12.en: (a) Since Christ is our virtue, the lack of His company and of union with the Father is sin.

31.2.13.en: (b) Virtue is the restoration of the nature of the soul, as the image of the Logos. And sin is the lack of this image.

31.2.14.en: (c) Virtue ascribes the soul to God as one of His children. And sin is its ascription to Satan. The soul that rejects its Father and its heavenly Bridegroom becomes forsaken like Jerusalem. Such a spirit easily becomes a prey to its enemies.

31.3.s.en: 4. God examines the ways of man

31.3.0.en: "Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?" [4]

31.3.1.en: In Job's examination of himself he declares that he speaks only by the witness of God Himself, who knows his conduct, his life, his thoughts, his feelings and all his intentions. The ways of man are laid bare before God, the visible and the hidden ways, for He is the searcher of hearts and reins.

31.3.2.en: When a man examines his depths, it befits him to realize this truth, that God is the examiner of his ways, not to catch his faults, but to sanctify him completely. God's concern even for our intentions and hidden thoughts consists of touches of surpassing divine love. For He desires to raise up even from our depths a living icon of heaven!

31.3.3.en: * Is not what he calls "ways" nothing but the ways of working? Therefore it is said through Jeremiah: "Amend your ways and your doings" (Jer 7:3)...

31.3.4.en: The Truth calls us to Himself [by walking in steps], saying: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden" (Mt 11:28). For the Lord commands us, "Come unto me," certainly not with the steps of the body but with the advance of the heart... So human works the Lord reckons as steps in the strict sense...

31.3.5.en: The prophet saw His exactness in examination when he said: "The Great, the Mighty God, the Lord of hosts, is his name, great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings" (Jer 32:18-19).

31.3.6.en: So (the Lord) praised the angel of the church of Pergamos in some things, and rebuked him in others, saying: "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith" (Rev 2:13). Afterward He says: "But I have a few things against thee, because thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam" (Rev 2:14). And it was said to the angel of Thyatira: "I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first. Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols" (Rev 2:19-20)...

31.3.7.en: Note how He records the good things and does not let them go without punishment for the evil things that call for cutting off. This truly happens because He sees the ways of everyone and holds them to account for their steps...

31.3.8.en: The saints themselves bind themselves to the strictest scrutiny of the thought of the heart, seeing that the heavenly Judge examines their life with all exactness, and so they test the mind in the depths of the depths, watching lest they be carrying any wrong thought.

31.4.0.en: "If I have walked with vanity, or if my foot hath hasted to deceit" [5].

31.4.1.en: After Job spoke of his care to sanctify his glances so as not to lose the eternal inheritance, he speaks of sanctifying the tongue, for he takes care not to utter a word of falsehood or deceive with his tongue, speaking what contradicts what is in his heart.

31.4.2.en: If God is the Truth, and is simple, with no deceit or crookedness in Him, then whoever takes care to enjoy fellowship with the Truth must give the devil no place in him, who is called the liar and the father of lies (Jn 44:8), and is also called the deceiver (2 Jn 1:7) or the beguiler.

31.4.3.en: * Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God.

31.4.4.en: The liar is a stranger to God. And Holy Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, for he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 44:8).

31.4.5.en: So Satan was called the father of lies, while the Truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 6:14).

31.4.6.en: Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God by lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly want to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves against all lying, lest it separate us from the Truth and the Life.

31.4.7.en: Father Dorotheus * People use lying not as something fitting for them but as something foreign to them.

31.4.8.en: * Let no one deceive his neighbor, as the psalmist says here and there: "with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak" (Ps 12:2). For there is nothing that brings enmity more than deceit and malice.

31.5.s.en: 6. Let us be weighed in the Savior's scales

31.5.0.en: "Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity" [6].

31.5.1.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the balance here is the Mediator between God and men, for in Him all our merits are weighed in the balance of His love, even though we see in ourselves the weaknesses of our life.

31.5.2.en: We are weighed in His balances so that we may imitate Him in His life. As the Apostle Peter says: "Because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not" (1 Pet 2:21-23). And the Apostle Paul says: "let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:1-2).

31.5.3.en: Truly all humanity in the scales goes up; there is none justified before the all-holy God. But when we are weighed in the balance of truth, who is the Lord Christ our Savior, He covers us in Him, and we bear His righteousness, and by Him we are justified before the Father, and are counted the object of His pleasure. "But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 1:30).

31.5.4.en: * God has not made us merely wise and righteous and holy in Christ; He has given us Christ for our salvation.

31.5.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * If Christ is the way of the righteous, then Satan is the way of the wicked.

31.6.0.en: 7 "If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands; 8 Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out.

31.6.1.en: "If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands" [7].

31.6.2.en: Righteous Job believes in not tearing life apart into an inner life and an outer life; man has one life, and everything within and without interacts together. There is no separation between the glance of the eye and the inner insight, nor between what is in the heart and outward conduct. It befits the believer to be sanctified inwardly and outwardly, in his thought, feelings, heart, words and conduct.

31.6.3.en: He feared sins whether in practical conduct, where his steps would turn aside from the way of truth, or through the glance, so that his heart would turn aside because of his looks, or in the practice of injustice, where a blot would cleave to his hands.

31.6.4.en: * Look also at how, by keeping watch over the inner activity, he returned to training the outward members. If it happens that the heart covets something forbidden, the eye must be kept by teaching and discipline until it refuses to look at it... Let us look into our consciences through these points, and see the loftiness of this man in comparison with the lowliness into which our breasts have sunk. If it happens that he imagines improper things, he quickly rises to kill them while they are still in the depths of the heart, with the sword of holy zeal. He does not allow this imagination to turn into action... Sin is not allowed to turn into action if it is killed inwardly in the place of its birth.

31.7.0.en: "Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out" [8].

31.7.1.en: Job declares his commitment to walk in everything in the spirit of truth, for he who does not walk so loses the divine blessing, and sows and reaps nothing, but another reaps it and enjoys it. He has no fruit in his life or in his offspring, since [his offspring are rooted out].

31.7.2.en: * According to Holy Scripture we call the preaching of the words of life a sowing. The prophet says: "Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters" (Isa 32:20). The preachers of the holy Church are seen sowing beside all waters, as they offer the words of life, like the wheat of the heavenly Bread, to all peoples, far and wide.

31.7.3.en: The Truth says: "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me" (Jn 4:34). So if Job abstains from doing something he says: [Let me sow, and let another eat]. He says plainly: what my tongue utters I do not practice myself, but another does. For the preacher whose ways differ from his words sows and goes hungry, while another eats. For he does not feed on his harvest when his conduct is wrong, when it does not agree with the uprightness of his words.

31.7.4.en: And since disciples, when they often hear from their teacher what is good without works, perish because of their conduct, he rightly added: "yea, let my offspring be rooted out" [8].

31.8.0.en: 9 "If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door; 10 Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her. 11 For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges. 12 For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase.

31.8.1.en: "If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door" [9].

31.8.2.en: After speaking of his flight from the evil glance, the evil tongue, deceit, caution regarding the way of the wicked, corruption of the heart and the practice of injustice, he speaks at greater length about fleeing from the enticement of the heart toward another's wife or falling with her into sin, for it is a grave crime. On the one hand it corrupts man's purity and chastity, and on the other hand it is an encroachment on the rights of the neighbor, and an intrusion into his bedchamber.

31.8.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that fornication differs from adultery (1 Cor 6:9), and that Job's heart was not enticed to fornication with a woman, and that he took care not to lie in wait at his neighbor's door and so commit adultery.

31.8.4.en: Job sees that defilement by fornication or adultery is a crime, and not merely a sin, though there is no one without sin. Job did not commit the crime of fornication or adultery, for it exposes a man to the court so that he may be sentenced to death. This crime is a consuming fire that destroys man's life and wipes out his fruits from their roots.

31.8.5.en: * The demon of fornication stirs up bodily desire, launches his attack on the ascetics, and strives that they abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.

31.8.6.en: And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to say and hear some (evil) talk, until it seems as though the (evil) deed itself were present before their eyes.

31.8.7.en: Father Evagrius the Monk * Is he counted to have been delivered from the sin of fornication in his heart, he who wanted to do evil with her because she was chaste?!

31.8.8.en: Is he not counted to have committed adultery in his heart with the harlot, he who sought her and did not find her in the brothel?!

31.8.9.en: St. Augustine * A brother came to Abba Matoes and asked him: "Is slander (or defamation) worse than fornication?" The elder said to him: "Fornication is worse." The brother asked him: "How can that be?" He answered: "Slander is a bad thing but can be healed quickly, for the slanderer often repents, saying: I have spoken evil and cruelly; but fornication of the body is death in his very being."

31.8.10.en: The Garden of the Monks * When night comes be vigilant that you are not drawn by bodily lust, but increase your prayer also as it leaves you. And if you are sitting and this lust attacks you anew, do not stay sitting for a long time but get up and pray. So also if the demon of fornication tempts you a thousand times, pray a thousand times with frequent prostrations, and God will rebuke the devil when you pray and he will depart from you.

31.8.11.en: Pope Theophilus * Abba Isaiah was also asked: [Why does fornication harm a man and press upon him so much?] He answered: [Because the devil knew that fornication makes us naked of the Holy Spirit. And hear the saying of the Lord: My Spirit shall not abide in these men, because they are flesh] [(Gen 6:3) LXX].

31.9.0.en: Abba Isaiah "Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her" [10].

31.9.1.en: He who breaks into his neighbor's bed to transgress against his wife falls into humiliation instead of the pleasure of bodily desires, for he becomes so poor that his wife is taken from him as a slave who works in the houses of others, doing the work of slaves and maidservants, such as grinding grain, which is hard labor. And as a slave she cannot prevent her master from having bodily relations with her.

31.9.2.en: A bitter picture of the sin of adultery, which robs a man of his freedom and dignity and the purity of his wife, and brings him into the humiliation of slaves.

31.10.0.en: "For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges" [11].

31.10.1.en: He who breaks in upon his neighbor's wife deserves death (Gen 38:24).

31.11.0.en: "For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase" [12].

31.11.1.en: Job compares adultery to the fire that consumes everything belonging to the adulterer, rooting out all the fruits of his labor and striving until he becomes poor, and even destroying his soul so that he perishes.

31.11.2.en: The Apostle John distinguishes between two kinds of sins: "There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it. All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death" (1 Jn 5:16-17). Perhaps he means by the sin not unto death the involuntary human weakness committed without knowledge, while the sin unto death is persistence in sin knowingly, in stubbornness and determination not to repent. Such a sin is a destroying fire for those who commit it.

31.11.3.en: * When the great preacher described him who is qualified for the grace of the priesthood, he did not say: [if any man be without sin] but [if any be without crime] (cf. Titus 1:6). Who is without sin, since John says: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 1:8). By this distinction between sins and crimes it may be said that venial sins defile the soul, while crimes kill it. This is the reason for which he says of the crime of lust that it is "a fire that consumeth to... destruction" [12]

31.11.5.en: * If the lustful man knew the effect of his lust on the poor victim, he would not do what he does. If the fear of God is in him it prevents him from that, and natural compassion obliges him to change his mind. Without doubt he knows it, but in the way in which one who has experienced injustice personally knows it.

31.12.s.en: 9. The right of dialogue with all

31.12.0.en: 13 "If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me; 14 What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him? 15 Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?

31.12.1.en: "If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me" [13].

31.12.2.en: In wondrous humility righteous Job gave his menservants and maidservants not only their human rights, which the world at that time ignored, as he lived before the Law of Moses, but he gave them the right to dialogue with him, and even their right to defend themselves even if they put him in the position of the accused!

31.12.3.en: * O masters, be kind to your servants, as holy Job taught us, for there is one nature and one family of humanity. For in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Gal 3:28).

31.12.4.en: St. Ignatius of Antioch * Job was righteous and practiced every human virtue, and did not abstain from one vice while clinging to another. We too count the weight just if it is a true and comprehensive weight, so that we do not weigh gold uprightly and lead otherwise, but our weights for all materials are honest, every weight like the other with justice in every case. This is the way by which Job was righteous and just in all cases, not only with regard to money and matter, but he kept this equality in all matters without exaggeration in measures. He avoided that vice with great care. Here he says: [If I rejected the right of my manservant and maidservant in their complaint against me, or supposed in myself that I was not of human birth like them] (Job 31:13, 15).

31.12.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * He who does not refuse to be judged together with his menservants and maidservants shows clearly that pride against his fellows has not at any time swallowed him up...

31.12.6.en: Behold, you see how he appeared lofty in his authority among the rulers in a wondrous way, and yet he holds dialogue with his servants.

31.12.7.en: In the assembly of the rulers he remembers his work, and in his dialogue with his servants he remembers that he is a creature (like them). He sees himself a servant under the true Master, and so he did not exalt himself with a haughty heart over his servants.

31.12.9.en: "What then shall I do when God riseth up?"

31.13.0.en: "And when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?" [14]

31.13.1.en: There was no written Law, nor laws protecting menservants and maidservants, but the faith of righteous Job in God the Judge, who is no respecter of persons, moved him to esteem every person, even if he was a servant of his.

31.13.2.en: * He who thinks of the coming Judge prepares his accounts for the better day after day without ceasing. He who looks to the eternal Lord with a trembling heart is bound to put a limit to his temporary lordship over those under him. For he looks well to the fact that there is no way for him to be above others temporally, because of the account he will give as one under Him who exercises authority without end. He knows who are under him, so it befits him to know that One (the Lord) who is himself over him, and by knowing the true Master, the vanity of his lordship, which bears vanity, dies in him. So blessed Job, fearing the judgment of Him who is over all, exercised temporary judgment as one equal to his servants.

31.13.4.en: * He who seeks the Lord with pain of heart, his petition is heard, if he asks with knowledge and care and a sorrowful heart, and is bound to nothing of the world except himself alone, in order to present it before the Lord without blemish as far as he is able. Like a lowly, despised man eager to please God his Lord, for if a man performed many wonders and healed difficult diseases, and had knowledge of all the sciences, yet as long as he has fallen into sin he cannot be without care for it, for he is still in repentance. And if he sees a man with all sins and negligence and judges him and despises him, let him know that his repentance is of no avail, for he has cast off from him a member of Christ and condemned him, and has not left the judgment to the Lord the Judge.

31.14.0.en: Abba Isaiah "Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?" [15]

31.14.1.en: * For persons who hold authority, the great work of humility is to keep in their thoughts the equality of creation. For we men are all equal by nature, but the distribution of the dispensation has been added to us so that we appear to have authority over certain persons. If we set aside our imagining of what happens temporarily (that we have authority over others), we shall very quickly find ourselves what we are by nature...

31.14.2.en: By nature we were all born equal, and since the dispensation of merits is varied, some have become above others by a hidden dispensation. This variance, which was added to our nature through a defect, is rightly ordered through the judgments of God; therefore, since not all walk in this life in the same way, one is judged by another. But the saints do not look at the authority of their positions within themselves, but at the equality of nature, for they know well that our ancient fathers lived not as kings so much as shepherds of flocks...

31.14.3.en: Since man by nature rules over the irrational animals, and not over the rest of men, it was therefore said to him that he must be an object of fear to the wild beasts, and not an object of fear to men. When you seek to be feared by one who is your equal, you are swallowed up by pride against nature... Therefore when Cornelius bowed down to the shepherd of the Church, and saw that the honor offered him was more than he deserved, he hastened to point to the equality of creation, saying the words: "Stand up; I myself also am a man" (Acts 10:26). Who does not know that it befits man to bow down to his Creator and not to a man...? So also the angel, when John bowed down to him, confessed that he is a creature, saying: "See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren" (Rev 19:10).

31.14.5.en: * If we are masters, it befits us not to despair of our servants and so be harsh with them, but to learn to forgive their offenses...

31.14.6.en: Likewise Paul was not ashamed to call the servant his son and his bowels and his brother and his beloved, so it befits us not to be ashamed of them.

31.14.7.en: And why do I say Paul? For the Lord of Paul was not ashamed to call us His servants His brethren... See how He honored us, and called us His servants and brethren and friends and heirs with Him, and that we appear beside Him and are counted workers with Him, and that the Master Himself works to be a servant! Hear and tremble!

31.15.s.en: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

31.15.0.en: 16 "If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail; 17 Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof; 18 (For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb;) 19 If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering; 20 If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep; 21 If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate: 22 Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone. 23 For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure.

31.15.1.en: "If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail" [16].

31.15.2.en: Job believed in the Creator who creates all men in their mothers' wombs without distinction, who forms every embryo without partiality between one social class and another.

31.15.3.en: God permitted righteous Job to enter into this severe affliction and to reproach God openly so that all generations might learn how there were righteous men, even in the era before the Law, who by living faith, through the natural law, rose above many who lived under the Law of Moses, and even in the era of grace.

31.15.4.en: He lived free, not enslaving himself to the practice of injustice or cruelty. He longed to provide the poor with all their needs and all they desired, whatever it cost him. He did not allow a widow to beseech with her tears, but hastened to give to all as much as he could!

31.15.5.en: * [He did not deprive the poor of all their desire, nor did he make the eye of a widow seek for anything] [16]. Do you see how he avoided arrogance, walking in moderation, as a physician to all, a common harbor and shared refuge for all who were in distress.

31.15.6.en: He says: [all their desire]. This does not mean saying yes to this need and not to that, but not depriving them of any need without distinction, even if it was fraught with danger and very costly. Note that he helped those from whom he expected nothing: widows and orphans and those without help. He was not occupied with boasting and glory, but gave for God's sake.

31.15.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * By these words the holy man shows that he not only serves the needs of the poor, but also grants them their desire... He adds [or made the eyes of a widow wait]... For it is written elsewhere: "Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee" (Prov 3:28)

31.16.0.en: "Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof!" [17]

31.16.1.en: His compassion reached the point that he could not eat alone, so that he not only called his wife and children to eat with him, but at every meal looked for an orphan to share his meal!

31.16.2.en: It was among the manners of fellowship and the rules of custom among the Easterners to invite others to share their food. In some desert regions, after the food was prepared, a member of the household would stand on a high place and call out in a loud voice that someone should come and share the food with the household. Sometimes he would wait for the arrival of a guest he had heard from a long distance, to share the family's meal.

31.17.0.en: "For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb" [18].

31.17.1.en: The care he enjoyed even for the servants was not issuing from a binding law or deterring statutes, but it was a matter that touched his depths, issuing from a divine work within him. From his youth, while still not bound by family matters, he treated the servants in his house as his own children, practicing tender fatherhood toward them while still young.

31.17.2.en: Again he does not mention how he trained himself in compassion toward servants, orphans, widows and all who were in need, but counted that what he practiced he had received from God while still in the womb before his birth.

31.17.3.en: * He counts it an injustice to his compassion to eat alone what was created for the common people... But as for these surpassingly compassionate bowels, did he draw them to himself by himself, or did he receive them by the grace of his Creator? Let us know it. [But from my childhood compassion grew with me, and from my mother's womb it came forth with me] [18]. Although he undertook the matter by his own command (that is, his struggle) so that compassion might grow in him, it is clear that it was not in his power for it to come out with him from the womb. It is clear that he did not ascribe anything to his own goodness, since he bears witness that he received this through the gift of his Creator. He received the goodness he practices from his creation. By this he settles his praise of the Creator, for what he has he received from Him, and he did not receive his compassion from another.

31.18.0.en: "If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering" [19].

31.19.0.en: "If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep" [20].

31.19.1.en: His care for the poor did not stop at offering them food, but when he saw a man groaning from nakedness because of cold or heat, having no clothing, he did not wait for him to ask, but counted it a blessing to himself to give them costly garments from the wool woven from the fleece of his sheep.

31.19.2.en: * By not despising the poor man he showed the virtue of humility, and he also clothes him out of compassion. For these two virtues must cleave to each other, and be supported by their mutual action. With regard to the need of a fellow creature, let humility help compassion, and compassion help humility, in a way that when you see a person who shares your nature lacking the necessities of life, you must not cease to clothe him, neither without compassion, nor out of pride failing to honor the one you clothe.

31.19.3.en: James rebukes strongly: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?" (Jas 2:15-16). This is what John the Apostle advises: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth" (1 Jn 3:18). For tender love must always appear in fitting words and at the same time in the service of giving...

31.19.4.en: Paul says: "But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want" (2 Cor 8:14). This means that in our concern we consider those whom we now see in want as ones we see some day in plenty, and we who are seen in plenty, if we neglect giving, will some day be in want...

31.19.5.en: Now he who is without a garment is less in need than he who is without humility. Therefore, when we see those who are sharers with us in our nature lacking outward things, let us consider our own lack of many great things within us, so that the thoughts of our hearts may not be puffed up against the poor. Thus we shall see with a penetrating eye that we ourselves are in truth in greater want with regard to our inner need. Blessed Job says well in this: [If I despised a passer-by because he had no clothing], for he shows compassion to the fellow creature unknown to him, since he calls him a "passer-by."

31.20.0.en: "If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate" [21].

31.20.1.en: Job did not take advantage of his position as ruler and judge, lifting his hand in injustice against an orphan.

31.20.2.en: * [If I have lifted up my hand against an orphan, I would not have seen myself the most exalted at the gate] [21]. The custom was that the elders sat at the gate to settle disputes during judicial sessions, so that everyone in the city might be in harmony, and no one might enter it at odds with another. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: "Establish judgment in the gate" (Amos 5:15)...

31.20.3.en: It is as though he were saying: even when I see myself, justly, as the best of those who exercise judgment, I do not take advantage of that for my own benefit by using my authority over the orphan.

31.21.0.en: "Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone" [22].

31.21.1.en: If the arm signifies work, then the man who wants to work by himself, ignoring his unity with his brethren, is like one whose shoulder, which joins the arm to the body, has fallen off, so that he cannot do what befits him as a living member in the body of Christ. Our holy dealings will not be accomplished without our union together as a holy Church, and at the same time through our personal relationship with God.
